vignette: Leilani had always been a pillar of strength in her community, working tirelessly as a social ministry worker to support those in need. But it was during a charity gala three years ago that her life took a devastating turn. A respected colleague, someone she had considered a friend, sexually assaulted her in the dimly lit hallway of the event venue. The memory of that night still played like a film in her mind, vivid and unrelenting: the feeling of his hands on her skin, the sound of her own voice whispering "no" as if from outside her body. Since then, Leilani had become increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings where she might encounter people who reminded her of her attacker. She was especially wary of men who shared similar features or mannerisms, finding herself constantly on edge around them. Even happy moments, like watching a sunset with her husband or laughing with friends, could quickly curdle into discomfort and unease. On those occasions, Leilani would excuse herself to find a quiet spot near the exit, where she could collect her thoughts and feel more in control. As time passed, these coping mechanisms became second nature to Leilani. She began to overeat as a way to manage her distress, using food as a temporary escape from the anxiety that gnawed at her. Heavy makeup also became a staple of her daily routine, helping her to present a mask of confidence and composure to the world even when she felt like crumbling inside. But these strategies offered only fleeting relief, and soon Leilani found herself trapped in a cycle of hypervigilance, constantly scanning her surroundings for potential threats. Her body had become a tightly coiled spring, always on the verge of reacting to some perceived danger. She would repeatedly check that doors and windows were locked, even when she knew it was irrational. The feeling of being constantly "on" left her exhausted, yet unable to relax even in the safety of her own home. Her memories of the assault replayed like a cruel mantra, reminding her that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined her as a person. Leilani couldn't shake the conviction that there was something fundamentally wrong with her - that if only she were stronger or more capable, the assault would never have happened. She compared herself unfavorably to others, convinced that they would have been able to prevent such an event from occurring. This toxic self-talk reinforced her need for control and safety, driving her to maintain a safe distance from people and situations that might trigger another flashback. As Leilani navigated this treacherous landscape of memories and emotions, she found herself retreating further into her shell. Her relationships began to suffer, including the one with her husband, who grew increasingly frustrated by her avoidance behaviors and emotional withdrawal. It was only when their marriage reached a breaking point that Leilani realized she needed help - not just for herself, but for those around her who were struggling to cope with her trauma. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Leilani finally sought out therapy, acknowledging the deep-seated fears and negative self-appraisals that had come to define her life. She knew it wouldn't be easy to confront these demons head-on, but she was determined to break free from the suffocating grip of her memories and reclaim the person she once was - a social ministry worker with a heart full of compassion, not a shell of fear and anxiety.
